summary: The note describes the Wheelabrator Incinerator, a waste-to-energy incinerator in Baltimore, Maryland, operating since 1985 and known formally as BRESCO. It has a 64.5-megawatt generating capacity and a tall white smokestack that is a landmark near Interstate 95. The note covers its air pollution controversies, a 2010 permit intervention by environmental groups and the EPA, a 2011 Environmental Integrity Project report on emissions, and its 2018 sale to Macquarie Infrastructure Partners. Parts of the source text are truncated.
one_line: A Baltimore waste-to-energy incinerator, operating since 1985, whose air pollution and permit disputes have drawn environmental scrutiny.
key_facts: The Wheelabrator Incinerator is a waste-to-energy incinerator in Baltimore, Maryland, US.
The incinerator is operated by Wheelabrator Technologies, a subsidiary of Energy Capital Partners.
The incinerator has an electric generation capacity of 64.5 megawatts.
On October 2, 2018, Energy Capital Partners announced the agreement to sell Wheelabrator Technologies to Macquarie Infrastructure Partners, a subsidiary of Macquarie Group.
The incinerator has been in operation since 1985.
The incinerator is formally known as BRESCO (Baltimore Refuse Energy Systems Co.).
The incinerator's tall white smokestack is a distinctive landmark for travelers on Interstate 95 and Washington Parkway.

In 2010, the Environmental Integrity Project, the Baltimore Harbor Waterkeeper, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network, and Clean Water Action intervened in the Wheelabrator Incinerator's permit-renewal process.
The 2010 intervention prompted the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to order the Maryland Department of the Environment to reinforce the plant's pollution-control permit terms.
According to a 2011 report by the Environmental Integrity Project, the Wheelabrator Incinerator produces greenhouse gas emissions per hour of energy than each of the state's four largest coal plants.
The incinerator also produces nitrogen oxide emissions.
Peterson stated: "This is excellent news for cleaner air and cleaner water in Maryland."
Peterson stated: "Without monitoring of emissions, we are really flying blind—neither the public nor MDE can be sure what's coming out of the Wheelabrator stacks."
In 2021, the Wheelabrator Incinerator was Baltimore's "single largest standing source of air pollution."
